findings.passage: In 2021 Faist named that goal, "wanting to just be a working actor," and set it aside, and Kushner independently confirms the refusals had "nothing to do with size of the role."
findings.problem: Kushner (GQ, 2026) describes parts that friends offered "after West Side Story came out," which was December 2021. The refusals the Times reported in May 2021 came before the release. The article treats these as one set of refusals and dates Kushner's account to 2021. It repeats this in the synthesis ("in 2021, at peak demand, he turned down parts that didn't feel right") and in the Type 6 FAQ ("in 2021 he turned down parts for reasons a colleague says had nothing to do with their size"). May 2021 was also before the film's release, so "peak demand" overstates it. The pattern of refusing offers stands. The way the two accounts are joined does not.
findings.acceptance_test: The body, the synthesis paragraph and the Type 6 FAQ separate the May 2021 Times report (turning down offers before the release and setting aside the "working actor" goal) from Kushner's account of parts declined after the film came out. Kushner's account is described as corroborating the pattern, not as confirming "the refusals." No sentence dates Kushner's account to 2021 or calls May 2021 "peak demand" unless a source supports it. C60, C63, C96 and C111 match the new wording.

findings.passage: The quiet years followed two deaths, an overwhelming summer and a collapsed film, and his reasons run from stamina to fame to financing.
findings.problem: GQ says Sgt. Rock was a project he was "reportedly attached to last year," meaning 2025, and that it fell apart in prep. The collapse happened during the 2024-2026 gap. It did not come before it. "Followed" puts it before the quiet years.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence places the Sgt. Rock collapse inside the gap (for example "followed two deaths and an overwhelming summer, and included a collapsed film"). The body's order of events stays as it is.

findings.passage: plays Charles Trask, a quiet farmer who is dangerous when provoked, in Netflix's _East of Eden_, from John Steinbeck's novel.
findings.problem: The role description repeats Cultured's own phrase ("a quiet farmer who's dangerous when provoked") almost word for word, with no quotation marks or credit.
findings.acceptance_test: The descriptor is either quoted and credited to Cultured or rewritten in the article's own words (GQ's Steinbeck line, "a dangerous man, even at fifteen," is one sourced option).

findings.problem: The frontmatter citations no longer match the article. They include two videos whose material was cut and that support no claim: the Spielberg featurette (asZ5_hxcpDA) and the 2016 Broadway.com interview (lFGPADR4r5k). findings.passage: His own accounts credit other people: "honestly Zoe and Florence," he told [Cultured](https://culturedmag.com/article/2026/09/21/film-mike-faist-east-of-eden-interview/) in September 2026, meaning Kazan and Florence Pugh, a producer on the series.
findings.problem: This paragraph and the first half of "Two years out of view" string short quote fragments together with repeated attributions. "Kazan" appears four times in the East of Eden paragraph. The GQ reasons ("needing to recalibrate" amid "so much noise") are spliced quote by quote. These passages read like research notes. Also, "Saying no at the top" opens with Kushner's post-release account and then jumps back to the 2020-21 pandemic ("Circumstance pressed too"), which blurs the order of events.
findings.acceptance_test: Every sourced reason and attribution stays. The East of Eden paragraph and the GQ/Cultured paragraphs read as prose, with no more than two quote fragments per sentence. "Saying no at the top" runs in chronological order. Total word count does not grow.
